section_title: Why is a prisoner brought before such a prominent gathering?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, along with the commanders and leading men of the city. And Festus ordered that Paul be brought in. 24 Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man. The whole Jewish community has petitioned me about him, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer. 25 But I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he has now appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him. 26 I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry I may have something to write. 27 For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him.”

context_lines: Agrippa and Bernice enter the auditorium with great ceremony, accompanied by military commanders and leading people of the city. Paul is brought in at Festus’s order. The scene places one prisoner before an audience of people who hold public influence.

Festus explains that demands for Paul’s death have come from the Jewish community in Jerusalem and Caesarea, yet he has found nothing deserving death. Paul has appealed to the Emperor, but Festus has nothing definite to write about him. He hopes the inquiry, especially Agrippa’s examination, will help him specify the case.

The governor’s report should remain distinct from a completed verdict or an exhaustive legal rule. He acknowledges the weakness of the case while continuing the process. The chapter ends with the reason for the audience assembled to hear the defense that follows in Acts 26.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly see a striking reversal of outward importance: the prisoner is about to give testimony before a king, a governor and influential listeners. The ceremony does not make their understanding complete, and Paul’s chains do not make his message false. The hearing must still be assessed by what is said and whether it is true.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 9:15–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/9.htm) describes Paul’s calling to bear Jesus’ name before Gentiles, kings and the people of Israel, alongside suffering for that name. This gathering gives that commission a concrete setting. Custody has brought the witness before a king and other public figures.

The pattern also recalls Jesus’ words in [Luke 21:12–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/21.htm), where appearances before kings and governors become opportunities for testimony. Paul’s next speech will use the opportunity to explain the risen Jesus and appeal to the people listening, not simply to display skill before a prestigious audience.
